checks.topic: Function types and their characteristic shapes, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes and end behaviour

questions.q: For f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - x - 6), the vertical asymptotes are:
options: x = 3 only; the factor (x + 2) cancels, leaving a hole at (-2, 4/5)
x = -2 and x = 3, since both make the denominator zero
x = -2 and x = 2, since these are where the numerator vanishes
none, because the numerator and denominator share a common factor
questions.concept: A denominator zero gives a vertical asymptote only if it survives cancelling
questions.why: Factoring gives (x-2)(x+2)/((x-3)(x+2)); the (x+2) cancels, so x = -2 is a removable hole at height (-2-2)/(-2-3) = 4/5, and only x = 3 sends the function to plus or minus infinity. Option 2 reads the unfactored denominator; option 3 confuses zeros of the numerator (x-intercepts) with asymptotes; option 4 over-generalises the cancellation, since only the shared factor is removed and x = 3 is untouched.

questions.q: f(x) = (2x^3 - x)/(5x^2 + 4). Which is correct?
options: Horizontal asymptote y = 2/5, the ratio of the leading coefficients
Horizontal asymptote y = 0, since the function is a proper fraction
No asymptotes at all, since 5x^2 + 4 is never zero
No horizontal asymptote; the degree of the numerator exceeds that of the denominator by one, and long division gives the oblique asymptote y = (2/5)x
questions.concept: Which asymptote you get is decided by comparing degrees, not by taking a ratio automatically
questions.why: deg N = 3 and deg D = 2, so the ratio 2/5 is not a horizontal asymptote; dividing gives f(x) = (2/5)x - (13/5)x/(5x^2 + 4), and the remainder term approaches 0, so the graph hugs the line y = (2/5)x. Option 1 misapplies the equal-degrees rule; option 2 misapplies the deg N < deg D rule; option 3 assumes that no vertical asymptote means no asymptotes, but end behaviour is a separate question.

questions.q: f(x) = x^3 + 1. Which statement is correct?
options: Odd, because the highest power of x is odd, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin
Neither: f(-x) = -x^3 + 1, which is neither f(x) nor -f(x); the +1 lifts the odd graph of x^3 off the origin
Even, because f(-x) = -x^3 + 1 differs from f(x) only by a sign
Odd, because f(x) - 1 = x^3 is odd and a constant term cannot affect symmetry
questions.concept: Symmetry is decided by computing f(-x), not by inspecting the powers
questions.why: f(-x) = -x^3 + 1 differs from f(x) = x^3 + 1 and also from -f(x) = -x^3 - 1, so the function is neither even nor odd. Options 1 and 4 both assume symmetry is a property of the x-terms alone, but a vertical shift moves the centre of rotation away from the origin. Option 3 misstates the even condition, which is f(-x) = f(x) exactly.

questions.q: For f(x) = -2x^4 + 7x^3 - 5, the end behaviour is:
options: f(x) approaches +infinity as x approaches -infinity, and f(x) approaches -infinity as x approaches +infinity
f(x) approaches +infinity at both ends, since a negative x raised to the fourth power is positive
f(x) approaches -infinity at both ends: the degree is even so the two ends match, and the leading coefficient is negative so both point downwards
f(x) approaches -5 at both ends, since the constant term dominates for large |x|
questions.concept: End behaviour is set by the leading term alone: parity of the degree plus the sign of the leading coefficient
questions.why: The term -2x^4 dominates; x^4 goes to +infinity at both ends, and multiplying by -2 sends both ends to -infinity. Option 1 is the odd-degree pattern; option 2 computes x^4 correctly but drops the -2; option 4 inverts the dominance, since the constant is negligible for large |x|.

questions.q: A student writes: 'f(x) = 4x/(x^2 + 1) has the horizontal asymptote y = 0, so the graph can never touch the x-axis.' Explain precisely what a horizontal asymptote does and does not claim, and say where this graph actually meets y = 0.
questions.concept: A horizontal asymptote describes behaviour only as x approaches plus or minus infinity, and may be crossed
questions.why: Model answer: saying y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote means f(x) approaches 0 as x approaches +infinity and as x approaches -infinity; it says nothing about what the graph does at finite x. Here 4x/(x^2 + 1) = 0 exactly when the numerator 4x = 0, that is at x = 0, so the graph passes straight through the asymptote at the origin, then rises, turns and settles back towards y = 0. Contrast a vertical asymptote, which genuinely can never be crossed because the function is undefined there.

questions.q: Explain what it means to say a graph is increasing on an interval and that it has a turning point at x = c, and explain why a turning point can never occur at a vertical asymptote.
questions.concept: Increasing/decreasing and turning points are statements about x-intervals of points that actually lie on the graph
questions.why: Model answer: f is increasing on an interval if for any x1 < x2 in that interval f(x1) < f(x2), so the graph rises from left to right; decreasing is the reverse. A turning point at x = c is a point (c, f(c)) on the graph where the behaviour switches from increasing to decreasing (local maximum) or from decreasing to increasing (local minimum). At a vertical asymptote x = a the function is undefined, so there is no point (a, f(a)) available to be a turning point; the graph runs off to plus or minus infinity there instead of turning back.

checks.topic: Coulomb's law statement, constants, vector form and sign conventions; the superposition principle; the electric field concept

questions.q: Two point charges q1 and q2 are clamped a fixed distance apart and exert a force of 6.0 N on each other. A third charge q3 is now clamped on the line exactly midway between them, without moving q1 or q2. The force that q1 now exerts on q2 is:
options: still exactly 6.0 N; q3 adds a further force on each of them but does not alter the q1-q2 force
less than 6.0 N, because q3 partially screens q2 from q1
zero, because q3 intercepts the field lines running between them
still 6.0 N only if q3 happens to be neutral; any charged q3 changes it
questions.concept: Superposition: forces are pairwise and additive, and charges do not shield one another
questions.why: Each pair obeys Coulomb's law using only that pair's charges and separation, so the q1-q2 force is untouched at 6.0 N; what changes is the net force on q1 and on q2, since a new term is added to the vector sum. Options (b) and (c) import the everyday idea of blocking, which has no counterpart in Coulomb's law - electrostatic force is not a beam that can be intercepted. Option (d) invents a condition: even a charged q3 contributes an extra force rather than modifying an existing one.

questions.q: The vector form of Coulomb's law is F_12 = (k q1 q2 / r_12^2) r-hat_12, where F_12 is the force on q2 due to q1 and r-hat_12 points from q1 toward q2. You substitute q1 = +3.0 microcoulomb and q2 = -5.0 microcoulomb with their signs. The expression returns:
options: a vector along +r-hat_12, since the magnitude of a force can never be negative
a negative number that should be reported as a repulsive force of negative magnitude
the same vector you obtain by using the magnitudes and then reversing the direction because the charges are unlike
a vector along -r-hat_12 - q2 is pulled back toward q1, i.e. attraction, with no further sign reasoning needed
questions.concept: Sign convention in the vector form: the signed product carries the direction
questions.why: q1 q2 is negative, which makes the whole coefficient negative, so the force lies along -r-hat_12, pointing from q2 back toward q1 - exactly attraction. Option (a) confuses magnitude with the vector's component along r-hat. Option (b) treats the negative sign as a defective magnitude rather than as direction information. Option (c) is the commonest error of all - using the sign twice, once in the algebra and again by inspection, which flips the direction back to repulsion. Use signed charges or magnitudes-plus-inspection, never both.

questions.q: A test charge of +2.0 nC placed at point P feels a force of 8.0 x 10^-6 N. It is removed and a -6.0 nC charge is placed at exactly the same point P, with the source charges untouched. The electric field at P is now:
options: three times larger and reversed in direction
unchanged in both magnitude and direction
the same magnitude but reversed in direction
zero, because a negative charge cannot define a field
questions.concept: The electric field is a property of the source charges and of the point, not of the probe
questions.why: E = F/q0 is a ratio: putting a bigger or oppositely signed charge at P changes the force it feels in exactly the same proportion, leaving E = 4.0 x 10^3 N/C in the same direction. Options (a) and (c) confuse the field with the force on the new charge, which does indeed grow threefold and reverse. Option (d) mistakes the sign of the probe for the existence of the field.

questions.q: Which statement about the constants in Coulomb's law is correct?
options: k = 4 pi epsilon-0, so a medium of larger permittivity gives a larger force between the same charges
k = 1/(4 pi epsilon-0), so a medium of larger permittivity strengthens the force between the same two charges
k = 1/(4 pi epsilon-0), so replacing the vacuum with a medium of larger permittivity weakens the force between the same two charges at the same separation
questions.concept: k = 1/(4 pi epsilon-0): permittivity sits in the denominator
questions.why: Because epsilon-0 (or epsilon for a medium) is in the denominator, a larger permittivity gives a smaller constant and therefore a weaker force - the medium permits the field more readily and screens the interaction. Option (a) inverts the relationship; option (b) has the correct formula but reads the inverse dependence backwards, which is the real discriminator here; option (d) swaps the two numerical values and their units.

questions.q: Superposition is always stated as a vector sum, never as a sum of magnitudes. Explain why, and describe one specific arrangement of three charges in which the net force on one of them is smaller than the force either of the other two would exert on it alone.
questions.concept: Superposition is a vector sum, so direction is part of the addition
questions.why: Model answer: Forces have direction, and two forces of the same size acting in different directions do not combine to twice that size - the sum depends on the angle between them, giving anything from the difference of the magnitudes (opposite directions) to their sum (same direction). Concrete arrangement: put a +2 microcoulomb charge at the origin with a +5 microcoulomb charge at x = +0.10 m and another +5 microcoulomb charge at x = -0.10 m. Each outer charge alone would push the middle charge with a substantial force, but the two forces are equal and exactly opposite, so the net force is zero - smaller than either alone. Any arrangement with the two forces more than 90 degrees apart works.

questions.q: The electric field is defined using a positive test charge, yet the field of a negative point charge is drawn pointing toward the charge. Explain why. Then explain why that charge feels no net force from the field it produces itself.
questions.concept: Field direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge; and a charge exerts no net force on itself
questions.why: Model answer: By definition E = F/q0 with q0 positive, so the field arrow at each point shows which way a positive test charge would be pushed. A positive test charge near a negative source is attracted, i.e. pulled inward, so the arrows - and the field lines - point radially inward, terminating on the negative charge. As for self-force: the field a charge creates is spherically symmetric about the charge itself, so there is no preferred direction for it to push in; every element of that field is matched by an opposite one, and a net self-force would let an isolated charge accelerate itself, violating momentum conservation. A charge's field acts on other charges only.

checks.topic: The six problem-solving strategies: what each one is, the condition attached to it, and what distinguishes it from its neighbour

questions.q: A laptop will not join the office Wi-Fi. Technician A immediately reboots the router because it is nearly always the router, then moves to the next ticket without checking anything else. Technician B disconnects the printer and retests, then the desk phone and retests, then the laptop VPN and retests, until the connection works. Which names both correctly?
options: Both are trial and error; A simply performed fewer trials than B

A is heuristics - the decision was made without stopping to think about the next course of action, saving time and energy and accepting a possibly sub-optimal outcome; B is trial and error - approaches were implemented one after another until the failure was removed
A is means-ends analysis, because the desired end determined the means; B is heuristics, because B used a rule of thumb about peripherals
A is trial and error, because A made one trial; B is brainstorming, because B considered several possible causes
questions.concept: Heuristics vs trial and error
questions.why: The dividing line is not how many attempts were made but whether candidate solutions are actually implemented and tested. Technician B implements various approaches until a solution is arrived at, which is the course definition of trial and error. Technician A tests nothing: the decision is made without stopping to think about the next course of action, buying speed at the cost of a possibly irrational or sub-optimal outcome, which is heuristics. Option a is the common one-trial-still-counts error - A performed no trial at all, because A never checked whether the reboot fixed it. Option c misuses means-ends analysis, which requires the target to be broken into sub-problems. Option d misuses brainstorming, which is a group technique for generating ideas, not one person testing them.

questions.q: A student must find which of 4 fuses in a box has blown. A developer must find which of 3,000 lines of code carries a logic fault. Applying the course stated conditions for trial and error:
options: It suits both, because in both cases errors are recognised and removed through experimental trials
It suits the 3,000 lines, because a computer can run the trials quickly, while the fuse box calls for heuristics
It suits the fuse box, where the possible solutions are few, but is time-consuming and inefficient on the 3,000 lines, where many possible solutions exist
It suits neither, because the course states that trial and error does not always produce a rational solution
questions.concept: The suitability condition for trial and error
questions.why: The course ties trial and error to the number of possible solutions: useful where they are few, time-consuming and inefficient where many exist. Four fuses is few; 3,000 candidate lines is not. Option b inverts the condition and smuggles in speed of execution, which the course never uses as the criterion. Option d is the most tempting wrong answer because it quotes a real sentence from the course, but solutions are not always rational is stated of heuristics, not trial and error. Option a is true of the definition and irrelevant to the suitability rule, which is what the question asks.

questions.q: A ministry must cut the average city commute from 70 minutes to 45 within two years. Team A writes down that target, lists the obstacles it expects to meet (bus shortages, junction delays, fare-queue times), splits the target into those three sub-goals, and assigns the best-suited method to each. Team B redraws the city as a diagram of stops and connecting lines only, discarding road names, building heights and district boundaries, in order to see where the network is thin. Which is correct?
options: Both are means-ends analysis, since each reduces a large problem to smaller ones
A is abstraction and B is means-ends analysis: A abstracts the target into sub-goals, and B derives the means from the diagram
A is means-ends analysis and B is analogy, because B understands the city by treating it as a different but similar system - a diagram
A is means-ends analysis and B is abstraction: A keeps every sub-problem and solves each with the best possible approach, while B removes the attributes that will not help reach a solution
questions.concept: Means-ends analysis vs abstraction
questions.why: Both shrink the problem, which is why option a is tempting, but they shrink it by opposite operations. Means-ends analysis thinks about the solution beforehand, determines the best strategy from the issues that will be encountered, then breaks the problem into smaller problems and solves each with the best possible approach - nothing is discarded and every sub-problem must still be solved. Abstraction filters out the unneeded attributes so that all patterns that will not help reach a solution are removed, leaving a model; Team B is the London Underground case exactly. Option b simply swaps the labels. Option c mistakes a simplified picture of the same city for analogy, which requires a different system whose underlying principles match.

questions.q: A doctor must destroy a tumour deep in the body with a high-intensity ray, but one ray strong enough to destroy the tumour would also destroy the healthy tissue it passes through. The doctor recalls a general who could not march a whole army down one mined road to a fortress and so split it into small groups converging from many roads at once, and fires several weak rays from different directions that meet at the tumour. Which is correct?
options: This is abstraction: the doctor filtered out the unneeded attributes of the medical problem to concentrate on the important ones
This is analogy, and it is sound because the two situations share surface features - both involve attacking a target
This is analogy, and it is sound because the underlying principle is the same in both: a force too destructive to apply in one piece can be divided into weak parts that converge on the target
This is trial and error: the doctor tried one strong ray, and when that failed, tried several weak ones
questions.concept: Analogy rests on underlying principles, not surface similarity
questions.why: The course defines analogy as using previously existing understanding to understand a new similar system as long as the underlying principles are the same. Option b states the right strategy for the wrong reason and is the answer that separates the student who memorised the word from the student who understood the constraint: both involve a target is a surface feature shared by countless situations that would give the doctor no usable idea, whereas dividing a force too strong to apply whole into converging weak parts is the structure that actually transfers. Option a fails because nothing was filtered out of the medical problem - understanding was imported from outside it. Option d fails because no strong ray was ever fired, so nothing was tried and rejected.

questions.q: A team lead gathers six colleagues to find the causes of a delivery delay. After each suggestion she says no, that cannot be it, we checked that last year. The hour yields six ideas, and she concludes that brainstorming does not work for her team. Using the course account of brainstorming, explain what she actually ran, name the two rules of brainstorming she broke, and state what the course says other people ideas are for.
questions.concept: Brainstorming and its rules
questions.why: What she ran was an evaluation meeting, not brainstorming. Brainstorming is a group-focused technique in which people come together and generate various solutions spontaneously, and the course attaches two rules to it: avoid criticism of ideas, and gather as many ideas as possible. She broke both - criticising each suggestion as it arrived, which is precisely what suppresses spontaneous generation, and thereby ending the hour with six ideas rather than the largest possible set. Her conclusion is therefore unfounded, because the strategy was never applied. The course also states that other people ideas can be fine-tuned: an idea value in brainstorming is not whether it is correct as offered but that it is raw material others can refine, so we checked that last year is a reason to develop the idea in a later evaluation stage, not to delete it during generation.

questions.q: The course says abstraction produces a model. Explain precisely what is removed and what is kept in forming that model, why an abstraction that removed the wrong attributes would still look like a successful abstraction to the person who made it, and how that risk differs from the risk carried by analogy.
questions.concept: Abstraction and the model
questions.why: In abstraction you remove the unneeded attributes of the problem - all the aspects or patterns that will not help you arrive at a solution - and keep the parts that bear on the solution, and what remains is an essential idea of what the problem is and how to solve it, called a model. The risk is that the model is judged only against itself: once an attribute has been discarded it is invisible, so the abstraction feels clean and workable exactly as a good one does. The Underground map looks perfect until you need walking distance between two stations, which the map deliberately does not carry. A faulty abstraction therefore fails silently and only reappears as a wrong solution to the real problem later. Analogy carries a different risk: it does not delete anything, it imports understanding from a second system, so its failure mode is choosing an analogue whose underlying principles are not the same - a surface match. Abstraction fails by dropping something that mattered; analogy fails by borrowing from something that never matched.

checks.topic: Constructing sketches, sign charts, and solving equations and inequalities graphically and algebraically

questions.q: The solution set of (x + 1)/(x - 3) <= 2 is:
options: x <= 7, obtained by multiplying both sides by (x - 3)
[7, infinity)
(-infinity, 3) union [7, infinity)
questions.concept: Never multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown; collect on one side over a common denominator instead
questions.why: Subtracting gives (x + 1 - 2x + 6)/(x - 3) = (7 - x)/(x - 3) <= 0, that is (x - 7)/(x - 3) >= 0, with critical values 3 (undefined, excluded) and 7 (zero, included). Testing x = 0 gives (-7)/(-3) > 0, x = 5 gives (-2)/2 < 0, x = 8 gives 1/5 > 0. Option 1 is the forbidden move: it silently assumes x - 3 > 0 and even then loses the x < 3 branch. Option 2 keeps only the right-hand branch and forgets that every x below 3 makes the left side negative. Option 4 reads the sign chart with the inequality reversed and wrongly includes 3.

questions.q: The solution set of (x - 1)^2 (x + 2) > 0 is:
options: (-2, 1) union (1, infinity)
(-2, infinity)
(-infinity, -2) union (1, infinity)
(1, infinity)
questions.concept: A factor of even multiplicity does not change the sign, but its root still makes the expression zero
questions.why: (x - 1)^2 is never negative, so the sign of the product is the sign of (x + 2), giving a positive value for every x > -2 except x = 1, where the product is 0 and the strict inequality fails. Option 2 forgets to remove x = 1; option 3 assumes the sign alternates at every root, which is the odd-multiplicity rule applied blindly; option 4 treats both roots as sign changes.

questions.q: How many real solutions has x^3 - 3x = 1?
options: 1, because a cubic equation has exactly one real root
2, because the line y = 1 meets the curve once on each side of the y-axis
0, because x^3 - 3x - 1 does not factorise over the integers
3: the curve y = x^3 - 3x has a local maximum of 2 at x = -1 and a local minimum of -2 at x = 1, and the line y = 1 lies strictly between them, so it cuts all three branches
questions.concept: Solving an equation graphically means intersecting the curve with a horizontal line, and the turning points decide how many intersections there are
questions.why: y = x^3 - 3x turns at x = -1 and x = 1 with values 2 and -2; a horizontal line at a height strictly between -2 and 2 meets the falling middle branch once and each rising outer branch once. Option 1 confuses 'a cubic has at least one real root' with 'exactly one'; option 2 ignores the middle branch between the turning points; option 3 confuses irrational roots with no roots, and factorising over the integers is irrelevant.

questions.q: The solution set of -x^2 + 4x - 3 > 0 is:
options: x < 1 or x > 3
x <= 1 or x >= 3
all real x except x = 1 and x = 3
questions.concept: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality
questions.why: Multiplying by -1 gives x^2 - 4x + 3 < 0, that is (x - 1)(x - 3) < 0, and an upward parabola is negative strictly between its roots. Option 1 is what you get by forgetting to flip; it is the solution of x^2 - 4x + 3 > 0. Option 3 is the complement with wrongly included endpoints, since the inequality is strict and the roots give 0. Option 4 treats the roots as isolated exclusions from an otherwise positive function, ignoring that this parabola opens downwards.

questions.q: For p(x) = (x + 1)^3 (x - 2)^2, explain how you decide the sign of p on each interval of a sign chart, and hence give the solution of p(x) < 0. Say explicitly what the multiplicity of each root does to the sign.
questions.concept: Sign charts and the role of root multiplicity
questions.why: Model answer: mark the roots x = -1 and x = 2 on a number line; they cut it into (-infinity, -1), (-1, 2) and (2, infinity), and on each interval p has one constant sign, so one test value decides the whole interval. Test x = -2: (-1)^3 (-4)^2 = -16 < 0. Test x = 0: (1)^3 (-2)^2 = 4 > 0. Test x = 3: (4)^3 (1)^2 = 64 > 0. The root x = -1 has odd multiplicity 3, so the sign changes across it and the graph crosses the axis; x = 2 has even multiplicity 2, so the sign does not change and the graph touches and turns back. Hence p(x) < 0 on (-infinity, -1) only, with the roots themselves excluded because the inequality is strict.

questions.q: You are asked to sketch f(x) = (x^2 + 1)/(x - 1). Explain how you find every asymptote, showing the working for the non-vertical one, and state the intercepts.
questions.concept: Asymptotes of a rational function: denominator zeros for vertical, degree comparison for the rest
questions.why: Model answer: vertical asymptote where the denominator vanishes and does not cancel, x - 1 = 0, so x = 1 (x^2 + 1 has no real factor to cancel). For the non-vertical one, deg N = 2 = deg D + 1, so there is no horizontal asymptote but there is an oblique one: long division gives x^2 + 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) + 2, so f(x) = x + 1 + 2/(x - 1), and since 2/(x - 1) approaches 0 as x approaches plus or minus infinity, the line y = x + 1 is the oblique asymptote. Intercepts: y-intercept f(0) = 1/(-1) = -1; no x-intercept, since x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution. Near the vertical asymptote, x approaching 1 from above sends f to +infinity and from below to -infinity.

checks.topic: PHY_102 problems: multi-charge superposition calculations, component resolution, equilibrium/null points, and ratio and scaling problems

questions.q: Q1 = +4.0 microcoulomb is fixed at x = 0 and Q2 = -4.0 microcoulomb is fixed at x = 0.60 m. A charge q3 = +2.0 microcoulomb is placed at x = 0.30 m. Each of the two charges alone would exert about 0.80 N on q3. The net force on q3 is:
options: zero, because the two source charges are equal and opposite
0.80 N in the +x direction
1.6 N in the -x direction, toward the +4.0 microcoulomb charge
1.6 N in the +x direction, toward the -4.0 microcoulomb charge
questions.concept: Collinear superposition: add the force vectors, not the source charges
questions.why: q3 is repelled by the +4.0 microcoulomb on its left (pushed toward +x) and attracted by the -4.0 microcoulomb on its right (pulled toward +x). Both forces point the same way, so they add: 0.80 + 0.80 = 1.6 N in +x. Option (a) is the trap - it cancels the charges (+4 and -4) instead of resolving the forces, and is what you get by never drawing the free-body diagram. Option (b) adds only one contribution or averages them. Option (c) gets the magnitude right but reverses both directions, i.e. treats attraction as repulsion.

questions.q: A charge at the origin is acted on by two forces from two other charges: 6.0 x 10^-3 N along +x and 8.0 x 10^-3 N along +y. The resultant force is:
options: 1.0 x 10^-2 N at 53 degrees above the +x axis
1.4 x 10^-2 N at 45 degrees above the +x axis
1.0 x 10^-2 N at 37 degrees above the +x axis
2.0 x 10^-3 N along the +y axis
questions.concept: Component resolution: Pythagoras for the magnitude, arctan(Fy/Fx) for the angle
questions.why: F = sqrt(6.0^2 + 8.0^2) x 10^-3 = 1.0 x 10^-2 N, and tan(theta) = Fy/Fx = 8.0/6.0 = 1.33, so theta = 53 degrees above the +x axis. Option (b) adds the magnitudes arithmetically (6.0 + 8.0 = 14) and guesses 45 degrees, the error superposition exists to prevent. Option (c) has the correct magnitude but inverts the tangent ratio (arctan 6/8 = 37 degrees) - the single commonest slip in 2-D problems, so check which component is on top. Option (d) subtracts the magnitudes, which is only valid for anti-parallel forces.

questions.q: A charge of +9.0 microcoulomb is fixed at x = 0 and a charge of -4.0 microcoulomb is fixed at x = 1.0 m. A third point charge placed on the x-axis experiences zero net force at:
questions.concept: Null point geometry for unlike charges: it lies outside the pair, beyond the smaller charge
questions.why: Between two unlike charges the force from one is repulsive and the other attractive but both point the same way, so cancellation there is impossible. Outside, on the side of the weaker (-4.0 microcoulomb) charge, the extra distance to the stronger charge can compensate: 9/x^2 = 4/(x-1)^2 gives 3/x = 2/(x-1), so x = 3.0 m. Option (a), 0.60 m, is exactly what you get by applying the like-charge between-them equation 3/x = 2/(1-x) - the right algebra with the wrong geometry. Option (c) puts the point beyond the larger charge, where the stronger, nearer charge always wins and no solution exists. Option (d) is the midpoint, which is only the null point when the two charges are equal and like.

questions.q: Two point charges separated by r exert a force F on each other. One charge is then tripled, the other is halved, and the separation is doubled. The new force is:
options: 6F
questions.concept: Scaling by proportional reasoning: F is proportional to q1 q2 / r^2
questions.why: The numerator changes by 3 x 1/2 = 3/2 and the denominator by 2^2 = 4, so F becomes (3/2)/4 = 3F/8. Option (b), 3F/4, comes from dividing by 2 instead of 2^2 - forgetting that the distance is squared. Option (a) tracks only the charges and ignores the separation. Option (d) multiplies by both charge factors as though they were 3 and 2 and drops the distance entirely.

questions.q: A student locates the null point between two fixed positive charges by placing a +1.0 microcoulomb charge on the line and solving for zero net force. She then repeats the calculation with a -3.0 microcoulomb charge and gets exactly the same position. Explain why the third charge's size and sign make no difference, and explain why the null point always lies nearer the smaller of the two fixed charges.
questions.concept: The null point depends only on the two source charges, because the probe cancels out of the equation
questions.why: Model answer: Setting the two magnitudes equal gives k|q3||Q1|/x^2 = k|q3||Q2|/(d-x)^2, and |q3| - like k - appears on both sides and divides out; the resulting equation contains only Q1, Q2 and the geometry. Changing the probe's sign merely reverses both forces at once, so wherever they cancelled before they still cancel. As for the location: the two forces can only oppose each other at a point between two like charges, and to balance a larger charge against a smaller one the point must be farther from the larger charge, since the inverse-square fall-off is what compensates for the bigger numerator. That places it nearer the smaller charge - and in a 9 to 1 case, three times as far from the big charge as from the small one, because the distances scale as the square roots of the charges.

questions.q: In a collinear three-charge problem, moving the test point from 1.0 cm to 3.0 cm from a source charge cuts the force to one-ninth, not one-third. Explain why. Then use the same reasoning to explain why, in a typical three-charge line problem, the nearer charge usually dominates the net force even when it is the charge of smaller magnitude.
questions.concept: The inverse-square dependence, and why proximity beats magnitude
questions.why: Model answer: The distance enters Coulomb's law as r^2, not r: tripling r multiplies r^2 by 9, so the force falls by a factor of 9. The force is not proportional to distance in any direct way, and three times as far so one-third the force is 1/r reasoning smuggled in from other formulas. The consequence for a three-charge line: the ratio of the two forces on the middle charge is (Q_near/Q_far) x (r_far/r_near)^2, so the distance ratio is squared while the charge ratio is not. A charge half the size but at half the distance produces 1/2 x 4 = twice the force of its larger partner. This is why you must always compute both contributions rather than assuming the bigger charge wins - and why answers should be checked by asking whether the net force sensibly leans toward the nearer charge.

checks.topic: Applying the strategies to stated problems: tracing a substitution puzzle, decomposing a target, choosing and justifying a strategy, and spotting where a strategy fails

questions.q: Trace this substitution puzzle. The two rules are: replace OB with BOOB, and replace BOB with O. Starting from BOB, which sequence actually produces BOOOB?
options: BOB -> BOOB -> BOOOB: apply the first rule to the whole word, then again
BOB -> O -> OB -> BOOB -> BOOOB: shrink first, then rebuild
BOB -> BBOOB -> BOOB -> BOOOB: grow by one rule, shrink, then grow again, never exceeding five letters
BOB -> BBOOB -> BBOBOOB -> BOOOB: grow twice to seven letters, then apply the second rule
questions.concept: Tracing a substitution puzzle; a derivation may have to grow before it shrinks
questions.why: Take it one rule application at a time. BOB contains exactly one OB (letters 2 to 3), so rule 1 gives B + BOOB = BBOOB. In BBOOB the only OB is letters 4 to 5, so rule 1 gives BBO + BOOB = BBOBOOB. Now letters 2 to 4 of BBOBOOB are B, O, B, so rule 2 replaces them with O: B + O + OOB = BOOOB. Option a misreads rule 1 as licensing BOB -> BOOB; the rule rewrites the substring OB, not the whole word. Option b dies at the first step: BOB -> O is legal, but a lone O contains neither OB nor BOB, so nothing can ever be applied to it again. Option c catches anyone who assumes a derivation should never overshoot the target length: BBOOB -> BOOB deletes a single B, and no rule deletes a single letter. That grow past the target then collapse step is exactly why there is no systematic method for deciding whether an arbitrary substitution puzzle comes out - nothing bounds how far the string may have to grow first.

questions.q: There are 50 questions in an exam. 2 marks are deducted for every wrong response and 4 marks awarded for every correct response. Bridget scored 165 marks. How many correct responses did she provide? A student sets c + w = 50 and 4c - 2w = 165, then tries every whole value of c from 0 to 50 and finds that none gives 165. What has this established?
options: Nothing yet; the search must be widened to allow unanswered questions, which will then produce a solution
6c - 100 = 165 gives c = 44.17, so the answer is 44 correct responses - trial and error merely lost the fraction

Every attainable score 4c - 2w equals 2(2c - w) and is therefore even, while 165 is odd, so no combination of correct, wrong and unanswered responses can score 165; the trials exhausted the candidates without ever explaining why, whereas one abstraction settles it at once
The trial-and-error run failed only because 51 candidates is too many for the method; on a shorter exam the same approach would have worked
questions.concept: Abstraction succeeding where trial and error can only exhaust
questions.why: Every correct response adds 4 and every wrong one subtracts 2, so any attainable score is 4c - 2w = 2(2c - w), always even. 165 is odd, so it is unattainable, and this holds whether or not every question was answered. Option a is the natural next move and still fails, because relaxing c + w = 50 changes nothing about parity - the constraint the student relaxed was never the binding one. Option b is the arithmetic-slip answer: 6c - 100 = 165 really does give c = 44.17, and rounding a non-integer into an answer is precisely the error the exhaustive trials should have warned against. Option d misapplies the course rule about trial and error: 51 candidates is few, so the method was legitimately applicable; it simply returns none of these without supplying the reason, which is its true limitation here. Trial and error can only report the outcome of the trials it ran, whereas abstraction, by filtering the problem down to the single relevant attribute (the parity of the score), yields the reason in one line.

questions.q: XYZ Corporation product quality is declining. Engineering lists 26 candidate causes across the manufacturing line. A junior proposes altering one input at a time and shipping a production batch after each change to see whether quality recovers. Judge this against the course.
options: It is a good plan: trial and error recognises and removes errors through experimental trials, which is exactly what a quality problem needs

It is trial and error applied where the number of possible solutions is not few, so it is time-consuming and inefficient; the case study instead begins with root cause analysis to identify the manufacturing process issues, narrowing the candidates before anything is changed
It is heuristics, and heuristics is barred from quality work because its solutions are not always rational; the case study begins by forming a cross-functional team
It is a poor plan because trial and error can never remove an error once introduced; the case study begins with brainstorming
questions.concept: Strategy fit judged by the course condition, not by the definition
questions.why: The junior plan matches the definition of trial and error perfectly, which is what makes option a so tempting, but a strategy is chosen by its condition, and the course states that trial and error is time-consuming and inefficient when the number of possible solutions is not few. Twenty-six candidate causes, each costing a full production batch to test, is the textbook case of many. The case study methodology begins with root cause analysis to identify the manufacturing process issues, then analyses customer feedback, quality records and production reports, and forms a cross-functional team, all of which shrink 26 candidates to a few before any change is made. Option c invents a prohibition the course never states and misnames the strategy, since nothing here is decided without thinking. Option d contradicts the definition of trial and error, whose whole point is recognising and removing errors through trials.

questions.q: A student is asked to write a program H that takes any program P plus P input, prints YES if P eventually halts on that input, and NO if P runs for ever. He plans to have H simply run P and print YES the moment P stops. Which is correct?
options: The plan is sound and only needs enough memory and a fast enough machine to be practical
This is a non-routine problem, so the student must develop a novel method by studying the problem critically, gathering information and implementing an effective strategy

The halting problem is undecidable - no algorithm returns an accurate true/false for every input value - and the student plan never prints NO at all, so it does not decide the question; it is not a systematic method
The halting problem is unsolvable, meaning no program halting behaviour can ever be determined, so H cannot be written and no individual P can be judged either
questions.concept: Decidable vs undecidable, and what unsolvable does not mean
questions.why: An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can give an accurate true/false for every input value, and the halting problem is the course named example. The student plan is not merely slow, it is not an algorithm for the problem at all: on a program that never halts it never returns, so the NO branch is unreachable and no answer is ever produced. Option a is the just-add-hardware error - the obstacle is not resources but that no systematic method exists. Option b is the sharpest distractor because it is a true-sounding sentence about a different category: a non-routine problem merely lacks a standard method and originality can supply one, whereas an undecidable problem admits no method however creative the solver. Option d is the misreading the course explicitly warns against: unsolvable does not mean no solution can possibly be found, since plenty of individual programs can be shown to halt or loop; what fails is the existence of a general deciding procedure.

questions.q: A student must complete a degree syllabus of 8 courses, each carrying 12 weeks of material, in 6 months, while working 20 hours a week. Set this out as means-ends analysis would: state the target, at least three sub-problems the decomposition produces, and for each sub-problem the approach you would pick. Then state the one requirement means-ends analysis adds that just break it into pieces does not.
questions.concept: Means-ends analysis - decomposition plus a chosen approach per sub-problem
questions.why: Target: 96 course-weeks of material covered and assessed within 26 calendar weeks, alongside 20 paid working hours a week. Means-ends analysis begins by thinking about the solution beforehand and identifying the issues that will be encountered - here a roughly 4:1 compression of material, a fixed weekly time budget, and eight assessments to pass. The decomposition might run: (i) Time budget - establish how many study hours per week actually exist after 20 working hours; approach: arithmetic scheduling, a routine sub-problem solved with a straightforward algorithm. (ii) Material triage - decide which of the 96 course-weeks are load-bearing and which are supporting detail; approach: abstraction, filtering out material that will not contribute to passing so a model of the syllabus remains. (iii) Sequencing - order the eight courses so prerequisites come first and assessment deadlines are met; approach: dependency ordering, a solvable problem naturally expressed as a graph. (iv) Recovery - decide in advance what happens in a week lost to work; approach: heuristics, since a fast good-enough rule beats a perfect but late plan. The requirement means-ends analysis adds: it is not enough to split the problem, because each smaller problem must be solved with the best possible approach, chosen in advance from the issues expected to arise, and every sub-problem must be solved, since it is the solving of all of them that solves the main problem. Plain decomposition stops at the split; means-ends analysis is answerable for the method attached to each piece and for the target the pieces must close.

questions.q: An online store checkout fails for roughly 1 user in 500; the cause is unknown and the team has drawn up 40 candidate causes. A junior engineer proposes disabling one feature at a time in production until the failures stop. A senior engineer says it is always the payment gateway, start there. Evaluate each proposal against the course stated condition for its strategy, say what each risks, and explain how abstraction could make the junior method viable.
questions.concept: Matching a strategy to its stated condition; abstraction as a precondition for trial and error
questions.why: The junior is proposing trial and error, whose condition is that the number of possible solutions be few. With 40 candidate causes, and a fault that shows only once in 500 checkouts, it is squarely in the case the course calls time-consuming and inefficient: each trial needs enough traffic to be sure the failure has really stopped rather than merely not recurred yet, so 40 trials could take months, and disabling live features risks introducing new failures that contaminate the very signal being measured. The senior is proposing heuristics, whose condition is that a sub-optimal solution be acceptable and whose payoff is saving time and energy by deciding without stopping to think about the next course of action; the course also warns that such solutions are not always rational. The risk is exactly that: if the gateway is innocent, the team has spent its effort on a confident guess and has learned nothing that narrows the remaining 39 causes. Neither strategy is wrong in itself; each is being asked to work outside its condition. Abstraction repairs this by changing the number the condition depends on: filter out every attribute of the failing sessions that cannot bear on the fault - browser chrome, page styling, user names - and keep what might, such as payment method, cart size, currency, network region, and whether the session was resumed. The resulting model of which sessions fail typically eliminates most of the 40 candidates at a stroke. Once the candidate set is genuinely few, trial and error becomes the right instrument, and the senior rule of thumb becomes what it should have been all along: one hypothesis inside that small set rather than a substitute for narrowing it.

recapCandidates.topic: The superposition principle: combining Coulomb forces and electric fields as vector sums
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Superposition looks trivially easy when it is stated - just add up the forces - and that is exactly why students lose marks on it. The word add hides the fact that the operation is a vector sum, so a student who has correctly computed every individual magnitude can still get the wrong answer by combining them arithmetically, or by cancelling the source charges (+4 and -4 look like they should give zero) instead of resolving the actual force directions. A second layer of confusion comes from the pairwise independence that superposition asserts: because everyday intuition says that objects in between block things, students expect a third charge placed between two others to reduce or screen the force between them, when in fact each pairwise Coulomb force is completely unaffected and superposition only adds new terms. A third layer is sign handling: the vector form already encodes attraction and repulsion in the signed product, so a student who substitutes signed charges and then also flips the direction by inspection uses the sign twice and reverses the answer. Finally the inverse-square weighting is consistently underestimated - the distance ratio is squared while the charge ratio is not, so intuition about which charge dominates is often wrong, and null-point problems get solved with the right algebra applied to the wrong geometry (between the charges for a like pair, outside for an unlike pair).
whyQuestions: Why is superposition a vector sum rather than a sum of magnitudes, and when is arithmetic addition legitimate?
Why does placing a third charge between two others leave the force between those two completely unchanged?
Why does the vector form F = (k q1 q2 / r^2) r-hat give the direction automatically, and why is applying like-repels-unlike on top of it an error?
Why can there be no zero-force point between two unlike charges, while for two like charges the null point must lie between them and nearer the smaller one?
Why does the location of a null point not depend on the size or sign of the charge you place there?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
States superposition as: the net force (or field) on a charge is the vector sum of the forces (or fields) each other charge would produce individually, each computed by Coulomb's law as if the others were absent - so charges never screen one another.
Shows the working method: draw a free-body diagram, resolve each contribution into components along fixed axes with explicit signs, sum the components separately, then recombine with Pythagoras and arctan(Fy/Fx) - never by adding magnitudes.
Handles signs once and only once, and applies the inverse-square weighting explicitly, noting that a factor in distance counts squared while a factor in charge counts linearly.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A +2.0 microcoulomb charge q0 sits at the origin. A +8.0 microcoulomb charge is at (0.30 m, 0) and a +6.0 microcoulomb charge is at (0, 0.30 m). Find the net force on q0. Both separations are 0.30 m, so r^2 = 0.090 m^2 in each case. Force from the 8.0 microcoulomb charge: F1 = (8.99 x 10^9)(8.0 x 10^-6)(2.0 x 10^-6)/0.090 = 1.60 N; all charges are positive, so q0 is pushed directly away from it, along -x. Force from the 6.0 microcoulomb charge: F2 = (8.99 x 10^9)(6.0 x 10^-6)(2.0 x 10^-6)/0.090 = 1.20 N, pushing q0 along -y. Now superpose as a vector sum by components: sum of Fx = -1.60 N, sum of Fy = -1.20 N. Magnitude: F = sqrt(1.60^2 + 1.20^2) = sqrt(2.56 + 1.44) = sqrt(4.00) = 2.0 N. Direction: tan(theta) = 1.20/1.60 = 0.75, so theta = 37 degrees below the -x axis (about 217 degrees measured anticlockwise from +x). Note that adding the magnitudes arithmetically would have given 2.8 N, a 40 percent error, and that the two forces are perpendicular here only because of where the charges were placed - in general every contribution must be resolved before it is added.

recapCandidates.topic: Rational functions: holes versus vertical asymptotes, the degree rules for horizontal and oblique asymptotes, and solving rational inequalities
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students meet rational functions as a list of separate rules and never see that all of them come from one idea: what happens to a quotient when the denominator gets small, and what happens when x gets large. So they set the denominator to zero and declare a vertical asymptote without first cancelling, drawing an asymptote where the graph in fact has a single missing point; they take the ratio of leading coefficients as a reflex whenever they see a fraction, producing a horizontal asymptote for a function that actually has an oblique one, or none; they treat a horizontal asymptote as a barrier the curve cannot cross, when it is only a claim about the far left and far right; and, worst of all in an exam, they treat a rational inequality like a rational equation and multiply both sides by the denominator, which is legitimate for an equation but not for an inequality, because the denominator changes sign across its own zero and the direction of the inequality flips on one side and not the other. The habits reinforce each other: a student who never factors first will never notice a hole, and a student who never draws a sign chart has no way of seeing that the solution set of a rational inequality usually comes in two disconnected pieces.
whyQuestions: Why does a factor that cancels give a hole rather than a vertical asymptote, and how do you find the height of that hole?
Why is the ratio of leading coefficients the horizontal asymptote only when the degrees are equal, and what replaces it when the numerator degree is one higher?
Why can a graph cross its horizontal asymptote but never its vertical asymptote?
Why is it wrong to multiply both sides of (x + 1)/(x - 3) <= 2 by (x - 3), even though the same move is fine for the equation (x + 1)/(x - 3) = 2?
Why does the sign of a factored expression change at a root of odd multiplicity but not at one of even multiplicity, and why is the root still excluded from a strict inequality either way?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Factor numerator and denominator first: cancelled factors give holes (height from the reduced function), surviving denominator zeros give vertical asymptotes.
Compare degrees for the far-out behaviour: lower gives y = 0, equal gives the ratio of leading coefficients, one higher gives an oblique asymptote found by long division; a horizontal or oblique asymptote may be crossed at finite x.
For an inequality, move everything to one side over a common denominator, mark the zeros of the numerator and denominator on a sign chart, test one value per interval, and include numerator zeros only when the inequality is non-strict while always excluding denominator zeros.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Sketch f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x^2 - x - 6) and then solve f(x) >= 0. Step 1, factor: f(x) = (x - 2)(x + 2)/((x - 3)(x + 2)). The factor (x + 2) cancels, so x = -2 is a hole, not an asymptote; the reduced function is (x - 2)/(x - 3), and the hole sits at height (-2 - 2)/(-2 - 3) = 4/5, giving the open point (-2, 0.8). Step 2, vertical asymptote: the surviving denominator zero is x = 3. Step 3, intercepts: the numerator of the reduced function vanishes at x = 2, giving the x-intercept (2, 0); f(0) = (-4)/(-6) = 2/3, giving the y-intercept (0, 2/3). Step 4, far-out behaviour: the degrees are equal, so the horizontal asymptote is y = 1/1 = 1; writing f(x) = 1 + 1/(x - 3) shows f approaches 1 from above as x approaches +infinity and from below as x approaches -infinity, and that f = 1 has no solution, so the graph never crosses that asymptote. Step 5, behaviour at the vertical asymptote: as x approaches 3 from below the numerator tends to 1 and the denominator to 0 from the negative side, so f tends to -infinity; from above, f tends to +infinity. Step 6, sign chart on (x - 2)/(x - 3) with critical values 2 and 3: at x = 0 the value is (-2)/(-3) > 0, at x = 2.5 it is (0.5)/(-0.5) < 0, at x = 4 it is 2/1 > 0. So f(x) >= 0 on (-infinity, 2] together with (3, infinity), minus the hole at x = -2 which must be removed because f is undefined there; x = 2 is included since f(2) = 0, and x = 3 is excluded since f is undefined there.
